title: The Array Method Toolkit: map, filter, reduce & friends
objective: After this lesson you will be able to replace loop-and-mutate code with readable map / filter / reduce pipelines, predict each method's exact return value and mutation behavior, and debug a chain by naming its stages.
why: Most production JavaScript is list processing: take a collection, keep the relevant items, transform each one, collapse to an answer — every React list, every API payload, every report is one of those shapes. The array methods are the shared vocabulary for that work: codebases that use them read as what happens instead of how to iterate, and a reviewer can spot the bug in a one-line filter that would hide in a ten-line for-loop. They also carry the two traps behind real outages: sort() mutates the array it is called on (your helper silently reorders the caller's data), and its default comparator compares strings, so [10, 9, 1].sort() returns [1, 10, 9]. This lesson makes those traps obvious — and the pipeline habit automatic.

blocks.text: Here is the same task written two ways: the total study hours of the published courses in a catalog. The loop is how everyone starts; the pipeline is where professional codebases live:

blocks.caption: Both print 36 — but the pipeline names its intents

blocks.text: Both versions compute **36** (8 + 12 + 6 + 10). The difference is what a reader — including future you, during an incident — can see. The for-loop mixes four jobs in one construct: managing an index, deciding which elements matter, doing the math, and accumulating a result. The pipeline separates them: `filter` says *which items*, `reduce` says *how they become one value*, and each callback receives the element under a name you chose (`c`) instead of `courses[i]` repeated five times. That dataset — six courses, four published, two drafts — stays with us for the whole lesson; every example from here on is runnable exactly as printed, in this course's JavaScript Playground.
map and filter: transform and keep

blocks.caption: map: one value in, one value out, always the same length · filter: a predicate decides

blocks.text: **map** runs the callback once per element and returns a **new array of the same length** — element *i* of the result is whatever the callback returned for element *i* of the source. The source array is never touched; if the elements are objects and your callback wants modified copies, build them fresh with a spread (`{ ...c, hours: c.hours * 2 }`) — returning the same object would alias the originals into both arrays. **filter** also returns a new array, holding only the elements whose callback return value is *truthy* — order preserved, possibly shorter, possibly empty. Notice that word: *truthy*, not *true*. `courses.filter((c) => c.hours)` keeps every course with a nonzero hour count and silently drops a 0-hour course — truthiness is the subject of the next lesson, and this is your first taste of why returning real booleans from predicates is a professional habit.

blocks.caption: reduce: (accumulator, element) => nextAccumulator, plus a seed

blocks.text: reduce is the general-purpose collapse. It walks the array carrying an **accumulator** — a value each callback invocation returns the next version of — and when the walk ends, the accumulator is the answer. The second argument is the **seed**: the accumulator's starting value. Trace the sum once: the callback runs six times, starting from `(0, courses[0])` → 8, then 20 (React Patterns added), 20 again (Node Internals is a draft — the accumulator just passes through), 26, 36, 36. The group-by example shows the real power: seed with `{}`, each step returns the updated object, and the result is an object — reduce can produce **any** type, which is why it can express everything the other methods express (and why a plain `filter().map()` chain is often clearer than one clever reduce — readability beats cleverness in code that changes).

blocks.title: The empty-array crash
blocks.text: `[].reduce((a, b) => a + b)` throws a `TypeError` — *reduce of empty array with no initial value*. Without a seed, the engine's only option is to use the first element as the accumulator, and an empty array has no first element. This is the classic 'works in dev, dies in prod' bug: the array was never empty in your tests. Always pass the seed — `reduce(fn, 0)` — and an empty array simply returns it, which for a sum is exactly the right answer.
find, findIndex, some, every: the question-askers

blocks.caption: find and some stop at the first match · every stops at the first failure

blocks.text: `find` returns the **first matching element** or `undefined`; `findIndex` returns its index or `-1`; both stop scanning at the first hit. `some` asks *does at least one pass?* and `every` asks *do all pass?* — both return real booleans and both **short-circuit**: `some` stops at the first truthy return, `every` at the first falsy one, so never rely on these callbacks running for every element (the `checked` array caught only three of six titles). One edge case deserves memorizing: on an **empty** array, `every` returns `true` — vacuously, nothing fails — while `some` returns `false` — nothing passes. That is logic, not a JS quirk, but it bites in features: `orders.every((o) => o.paid)` is `true` for a brand-new user with zero orders. Decide whether 'no orders at all' really means 'all paid' in your business logic before you ship that line.

blocks.caption: toSorted / toReversed (ES2023): the non-mutating twins of sort / reverse

blocks.text: Both traps are visible in the output above. The default comparator compares elements **as strings**, which is fine for alphabetical text and wrong for anything numeric — prices, priorities, ages, version numbers. A numeric comparator is `(a, b) => a - b` (a negative result puts `a` first); descending is `b - a`. The mutation trap is the sneakier one: `sort()` sorts **in place** and returns the very same array object, so `const sorted = list.sort()` *looks* like it creates a sorted copy — both names point at one array, and whoever handed you `list` now finds it reordered. The same is true of `reverse()`, `splice()`, `push()` and friends. ES2023 added the safe twins — `toSorted`, `toReversed`, `toSpliced` — which copy first and leave the source alone; every current browser and Node 20+ support them. On an older runtime, the idiom is an explicit copy: `[...list].sort(cmp)`.

blocks.title: sort() edits your caller's data
blocks.text: A helper like `function topThree(list) { return list.sort(byScore).slice(0, 3); }` does not just answer a question — it permanently reorders the array the caller passed in. If the caller logs that array later, or renders it in a UI, you have introduced a bug that appears *sometimes*, far from the code that caused it. Treat `sort` / `reverse` / `splice` as mutations of someone else's property: at function boundaries, prefer `toSorted(cmp)` — or copy explicitly with `[...list].sort(cmp)`.
flatMap: map, then flatten one level

blocks.caption: flatMap = map followed by flat(1) — the [x] / [] pattern is map + filter in one pass

blocks.text: `flatMap` runs the callback like `map` does, then flattens the result **one level** — no deeper. It exists for callbacks that want to return *zero, one, or many* items per element: return `[]` to drop, `[x]` to keep, `[x, y]` to expand. The `publishedTitles` line is a genuine map-and-filter in a single pass; classic real-world uses are splitting sentences into words (`lines.flatMap((line) => line.split(" "))`) or expanding one record into its tags. Deeper nesting needs `.map(...).flat(2)` or `flat(Infinity)` — flatMap only ever takes one level off.

blocks.caption: Each stage's output is the next stage's input
Same result — but now every intermediate is inspectable

blocks.text: Chains read top-to-bottom as a story: *keep the published ones, sort longest-first, format the labels*. Two habits keep them correct: **filter early** (why transform items you are about to throw away?) and **sort objects before mapping to strings** — once a course has become `"React Patterns (12h)"`, sorting by duration means parsing the number back out of the string. But chains are only readable while they are short. Past three or four stages — or the moment one of them misbehaves — break the pipeline into named intermediates like the second version: each `const` is a checkpoint you can log, each name documents a stage, and a bug can only hide between two adjacent lines instead of inside one towering expression. You can always re-fold the stages into a chain once the pipeline is proven; you cannot debug an expression you cannot see inside.

blocks.q: What is the difference between map and forEach, and when do you use each?
blocks.a: forEach is for side effects — logging, saving, updating the DOM — and returns `undefined`. map builds a new array from each callback's return value, so the result is the value. The tell is the callback's return: if you are computing something per element, use map. The pattern map exists to replace is forEach plus an array declared *outside* the loop that gets pushed into — that leaks the accumulator into the surrounding scope and invites bugs. Interviewers like the follow-up 'can map mutate the original?' — yes: if the elements are objects and the callback mutates them, both arrays share those objects. But the array *structure* — length and positions — is never changed by map.

blocks.title: Pipeline the catalog
blocks.note: Exact output: `React Patterns (12h) | Testing Web Apps (10h) | TypeScript Basics (8h) | CSS Layout Deep Dive (6h)`, then `total published hours: 36`, then `average: 9`. Predict all three lines before running. Then flip the comparator to `(a, b) => a.hours - b.hours` and re-run — only the first line changes.

blocks.title: The toolkit in six lines
items: map / filter / reduce replace loop bookkeeping with named intents: transform each, keep some, collapse to one — the callback receives the element by name, and each method has exact, predictable return semantics
map returns a new same-length array and never mutates the source; filter coerces its predicate with truthiness, so return real booleans
reduce always gets a seed: `[].reduce(fn)` throws a TypeError, `reduce(fn, 0)` returns 0 — an empty array should be an answer, not a crash
find / findIndex return the first match or undefined / -1; some / every short-circuit, and on an empty array every is true while some is false
sort() mutates AND compares strings by default — `[10, 9, 1].sort()` is `[1, 10, 9]`. Numeric, non-mutating order is `toSorted((a, b) => a - b)` (or `[...list].sort(cmp)` on old runtimes)

flatMap is map plus one flatten: return `[]` to drop, `[x]` to keep, `[x, y]` to expand; chain at most ~3 stages, filter early, sort objects before mapping to strings — and name your intermediates to debug

exercise.prompt: Build the quarterly catalog report from the `courses` dataset in three named steps. (1) `listing`: an array of "Title (Xh)" strings for the **published** courses, sorted by hours **descending**. (2) `totalHours`: their total. (3) `averageHours`: total divided by count. Verify: `listing[0]` is "React Patterns (12h)", `totalHours` is 36, `averageHours` is 9. Then answer one design question in a comment: why must the sort happen *before* the map to strings?
hints: Start with filter — every later stage only cares about published courses, so shrink the data first: `courses.filter((c) => c.published)` gives you 4 objects instead of 6.
Sort the OBJECTS while `hours` is still a number: `.toSorted((a, b) => b.hours - a.hours)` — descending means b minus a. After the map to strings it is too late.
Format last, with a template literal: `${c.title} (${c.hours}h)`. For the total, `reduce((sum, c) => sum + c.hours, 0)` — with the seed, an empty catalog answers 0 instead of throwing.
exercise.why: The pipeline order is the real lesson. Filtering first means the sort compares 4 objects instead of 6 and the reduce sums 4 numbers. Sorting while courses are still objects lets the comparator read `c.hours` directly — after the map, duration lives inside a string. And the reduce seed makes an empty catalog return 0 (a sensible 'no courses' answer) rather than a TypeError. Same tools as the lesson; the order is the engineering. One more trap avoided for free: `averageHours` divides by `published.length` (4) — computing it from `courses.length` (6) would quietly report 6 instead of 9.

options: [1, 9, 10] — numbers sort numerically by default
[1, 10, 9] — the default comparator compares strings, and "1" < "10" < "9"
[10, 9, 1] — sort returns a copy in the original order when no comparator is given
TypeError — numeric arrays require a comparator
quiz.explain: The default comparator converts elements to strings and compares them lexicographically: "1" comes before "10" (a prefix is 'smaller'), which comes before "9". Numeric sorting needs a comparator: `(a, b) => a - b`. Bonus trap in the same call: sort() also mutates the array in place.

quiz.q: const total = [].reduce((acc, x) => acc + x); — what happens?
options: total is 0 — the empty sum
total is undefined
TypeError: reduce of empty array with no initial value
total is NaN
quiz.explain: Without a seed, reduce wants to use the first element as the initial accumulator — an empty array has none, so it throws. With a seed (`reduce(fn, 0)`) the empty array simply returns the seed, the mathematically sensible zero. This bug is famous for passing every test and dying in production the first time the data is empty.

quiz.q: const a = [1, , 3]; let calls = 0; const b = a.map((x) => { calls++; return x * 2; }); — what are calls and b?
options: calls is 3, b is [2, NaN, 6] — the hole becomes NaN
calls is 2, b is [2, <empty>, 6] — map skips holes but preserves them
calls is 3, b is [2, undefined, 6] — the hole maps to undefined
throws — map cannot process sparse arrays
quiz.explain: Array methods skip holes entirely: the callback is never invoked for index 1 (calls is 2), the hole is preserved in the result, and `b.length` is still 3 (`1 in b` is false; JSON.stringify shows [2, null, 6]). To touch every index, normalize first with `Array.from(a)` — which fills holes with undefined — and then map.

options: false — no element passes the test
true — vacuously: no element FAILS the test
TypeError — every needs at least one element
undefined
quiz.explain: every asks 'can I find a failing element?' — over zero elements the answer is no, so it returns true (and some over zero elements is false, since nothing passes). Practical sting: orders.every((o) => o.paid) is true for a user with no orders. Empty-data vacuous truth deserves a deliberate decision, not an accident.

quiz.q: Which of these calls leaves `list` unchanged?
options: list.sort((a, b) => a - b)
list.reverse()
list.splice(0, 1)
list.toSorted((a, b) => a - b)
quiz.explain: sort, reverse and splice all mutate in place (sort and reverse even return the same array object, which makes them look innocent). toSorted is the ES2023 copying twin — it returns a new array and leaves the source untouched. On runtimes without it, `[...list].sort(cmp)` copies explicitly.

summary: The array toolkit turns iteration into vocabulary. map transforms (new array, same length, source untouched); filter keeps (new array, truthiness decides, return real booleans); reduce collapses to any shape you seed it with — always seed, because an empty array without a seed throws. find and findIndex answer 'which one', some and every answer 'does any / do all' and short-circuit (vacuously true and false on empty arrays); flatMap maps and flattens one level, with [] to drop and [x, y] to expand. sort carries the two classic traps — it mutates, and it compares strings — so `toSorted((a, b) => a - b)` is the professional default. Chains of about three stages read like sentences when you filter early and sort objects before formatting them; when one misbehaves, name the intermediates and log each stage.
next: Notice what decided every example in this lesson: quiet, implicit conversions. filter kept items whose predicate was 'truthy' — not strictly true; the sort comparator worked because subtraction coerced strings to numbers. What exactly is on the falsy list? Why does `"1" == 1` hold while `null == 0` does not? And why do `0 || 3000` and `0 ?? 3000` disagree? The next lesson is the missing manual: the complete falsy list, the coercion rules behind ==, and the modern operators (?? and ?.) that retire the old footguns.
